blocks.text: Elwin Tobing

About 25 years ago, I developed The Prospect, probably one of the first blogs in Indonesia that presented analysis of the nation's problems and future. One of the missiles, Daily Prospect, was inspired by The Daily Dich of Andrew Sullivan, who was a pioneer of political blogs that became one of the influential voices in the public opinion of the United States.
Why did I start?

Indonesia was still wrestling with the impact of the 1998 monetary crisis. The economy hasn't fully recovered yet. The political uncertainty and social conflict continue, including in Poso and Maluku. In fact, the senior political observer of Juandi wrote an article called Indonesia: A Failed State?
I'm trying to understand why Indonesia is so difficult to get out of crisis and build sustainable progress.
ALL IN THE MIND
My conclusion at the time: one of the problems essentially lies in thinking, or mindset.
And underneath the weakness of the mindset there are more fundamental issues: lower quality of literacy, which is closely related to the weak culture of reading and learning.

The first PISA results amplified my worries. In the 2000 PISA results expanded with the addition, Indonesia is rated 39 of 41 countries in reading, rank 39 in math, and the 38th in science. About 80% of our students don't understand what they're reading.

Indeed, PISA measures 15-year-olds' capabilities. However, the weak quality of education in the next generation makes it a serious warning about the intellectual capacity of the next generation, including the future leader and decision-making.
How can we build a developed country if the ability to read, understand problems, and think critically is still so weak?

Development is not just about capital, infrastructure, technology or policy. Everything matters. But his success depends heavily on the quality of humans who design, carry out, and respond to the development.
I remember Bill Guerin, the Asian Times journalist, who sent his contribution to the Daily Prospect, called All in the Mind. The message was simple: social life change began with a change of thought.

In 2002, I then developed the notion of Mindset Enhancing Campaign (MEC), a movement to enrich the way of thinking and the way of reason through school, college and public space. Unfortunately, it hasn't evolved due to limited time and resources. I was undergoing an important economic education in the United States.
25 years, same time.
Twenty-five years passed. What changed?

Indonesia has certainly made a lot of progress. The economy is growing, infrastructure is growing and technology is changing people's lives. However, the fundamental problem that I was concerned about a quarter of a century ago still feels strong today.
Mindset is still one of the great impediments of Indonesian progress.
A way of thinking that makes complicated matters go away. Feel knowing without really understanding. More confident in his own beliefs than evidence.
Defensive against criticism, reluctant to learn from fault, and more busy seeking justification than fixing things.
Who put formalities ahead of substance, loyalty rather than capabilities, as well as imaging rather than real results.
And most worrisome: a way of thinking which rejects reality and denial.
Not because the reality is not visible, but because we don't want to, or can't, read it clearly.
Why does this matter keep repeating?
I think one of the same problems is still the same: very weak quality of literature.

Look back at the PISA results. By 2025, about 75% of Indonesian students at 15 years old have not reached the minimum level of literacy. It can read but it doesn't understand what it's reading. Almost nothing reaches the highest level of literacy.
Indonesian reading scores even dropped from 371 on 2000 to 365 in 2025. Over the past two decades, the literacy crisis has not been resolved yet. Even relatively, worse.

Of course, low literacy isn't the only cause for Indonesian problems. The quality of institutions, management, political incentives, and economic structures are also very decisive. However, such weaknesses can be exacerbated by the low-level ability to understand information, judge evidence, and think critical.
We often argue about solutions before understanding the issue. Announcing success without testing the results. Defending policy without actually evaluating the impact.
And in fact, problem solving has always started with the ability to recognize problems properly.
We can't fix something we don't understand. It's even harder to deny the reality.
FROM DIAGNOSIS TO TRANSFORMATION
Twenty-five years ago, I tried to answer this challenge through MEC. Now, through the Literacy for Future (LIFT), I'm returning to the same problem with a more concrete approach.

Through storybooks, reading activities, school and family involvement, as well as critical thinking and character reinforcement, LIFT has been trying to build culture reading and learning since elementary school.

In the last less than a year, this initiative has reached over 20,000 students, especially in Jakarta. This is just the first step. Building culture of reading and thinking takes time, consistency, and involvement in many parties.
But we have to realize one thing: the literacy crisis is not just a school issue. It's a nation issue, across the entire layer of society, including leaders and policy makers.
Then, where should we start? Let's get back to reading. We're not done with the most fundamental issue yet.
Not just following social media gossip or rolling up nonstop Tickook. But it's reading the quality books, the writing that stirs the mind, and analysis that challenges our own beliefs.
Reading to understand, not just looking for justification. Learn to accept criticism, check facts, and see problems from different angles.
Because a nation that can't read reality will continue to have difficulty repairing its reality. Indonesia has no shortage of problems to solve. But we have to stop denying it.
Indonesia cannot afford to remain in denial.

(Elwin Tobing, Economic Professor, the President of INADATA, Irvine, US; Writing Book of The NOW or NEVER EMPs which gives the blueprint the transformative ecosystem of national innovation as an absolute requirement to 2050 Golden Indonesia. Elwin also developed the LIFT-Literacy Movement for Future and the NEXUS Program as an ecosystem transformed literacy, character, and scientific interest of Indonesian educators.
